L3@P0: Traders’ Concentration, Hedging Pressure, and Risk
L4@P0: Premium in Futures Markets
L5@P0: (Received Jul 04, 2022; First Revision Dec 26, 2022; Second Revision Feb 03, 2023;
L6@P0: Accepted Mar 20, 2023)
L7@P0: Purpose – This study explores the relationship between market concentration and risk premiums in the
L8@P0: U.S. futures markets from 2010 to 2018. When studying the determinants of risk premiums in
L9@P0: futures markets, existing literature focuses mainly on the risk-averse behavior of hedgers.
L10@P0: Design/methodology/approach – This study provides a new measure of market concentration, which
L11@P0: measures the amount of information content held by traders in futures markets.
L12@P0: Findings – 1. Market concentration and hedging pressure coexist in explaining the determinants of risk
L13@P0: premiums in various futures markets. 2. Market concentration and hedging pressures have no
L14@P0: short-term impact on futures risk premiums. As the holding period increases, the impact of market
L15@P0: concentration and hedging pressures on futures risk premiums will increase.
L16@P0: Research limitations/implications – Market concentration does not distinguish between commercial
L17@P0: and non-commercial traders, so the largest traders may be classified as either commercial or noncommercial traders.
L18@P0: Practical implications/Social implications – Market concentration provides an alternative measure of
L19@P0: risk premiums in the futures markets. For some futures products that cannot be explained by
L20@P0: hedging pressure, changes in risk premiums can be predicted through market concentration.
L21@P0: Originality/value – This study will provide a lot of practical help for market investors who set up
L22@P0: investment strategies and policymakers who establish trading rules to prevent market manipulation,
L23@P0: thereby helping establish a more efficient and fair trading environment in futures markets.
L24@P0: Keywords – Futures, Concentration, Risk premium, Hedging pressure

L35@P1: 1. Research Motivation and Purpose
L36@P1: In the financial market, issues such as international market instability and supply chain changes will frequently
L37@P1: cause changes to stock market prices, which can impact both weighted stock price indexes and individual stocks. To
L38@P1: respond to these unpredictable occurrences in the market, derivative financial products such as forward contracts, futures,
L39@P1: and options have emerged. As to the prices of these derivative financial products, regarding the futures market, the cost
L40@P1: of carry model proposed by Cornell and French (1983a, b) takes into account warehousing cost, as well as stock,
L41@P1: transportation, insurance, interest, and tax costs of products, then uses these factors to calculate the theoretical prices of
L42@P1: futures.
L43@P1: However, reality often differs from theory. The theoretical prices calculated by the cost of carry model are not
L44@P1: actually consistent with actual prices, implying that there are other reasons for such a discrepancy between futures and
L45@P1: spot prices. Past research findings have indicated that the difference between futures and spot prices in the futures market
L46@P1: is due to varying degrees of risk premium (De Roon et al., 2000). De Roon et al. (2000) pointed out that the measurement
L47@P1: of risk premium originates from the difference between future spot prices and current futures prices. Because in theory
L48@P1: future spot prices and current futures prices should converge, the return gained from futures products is a good
L49@P1: measurement index for futures risk premium. Consequently, this study used futures return as a proxy variable for risk
L50@P1: premium to explore the impact of hedging pressure and trader concentration on risk premium.
L51@P1: Discussion on futures risk premium can be traced as far back as the backwardation theory of Keynes (1930) and
L52@P1: Hicks (1939), where through researching the agricultural production market, it was believed that hedgers basically
L53@P1: assume a net short position in the futures market. This, as a result, will drive down futures prices, cause prices to fall
L54@P1: below expected prices, and lead to mispricing in the futures market. Because a large stock of agricultural products will
L55@P1: be harvested in the future, this will also result in immense spot pressure. On the other hand, the research of Houthakker
L56@P1: (1957) and Cootner (1960) believed that the backwardation theory can also be applied to the net long position, in which
L57@P1: case futures prices are driven above expected prices. In such futures contracts, speculators play the role opposite to that
L58@P1: of hedgers through taking risks and expecting to get positive returns. Therefore, speculators can cause deviated futures
L59@P1: prices to revert to reasonable, expected prices, an effect that forms the basis for the hedging pressure theory.
L60@P1: In continuation of the hedging pressure theory, the research of Dusak (1973), Black (1976), and Jagannathan (1985)
L61@P1: found that the net positions of hedgers in the futures market can be used to measure hedging pressure. Hedging pressure
L62@P1: arises from the fact that hedgers are reluctant to take on time and transaction risks. To secure future interests, they will
L63@P1: forgo the opportunity to obtain higher returns, and will either use the method of selling futures to guarantee personal
L64@P1: interest, or purchasing futures to avoid rises in raw material costs by way of fixing production costs. In addition, when
L65@P1: speculators expect that future spot prices will diverge from known futures prices, they will invest in the futures market
L66@P1: for arbitrage.
L67@P1: When constructing a model for impact on futures prices, Stoll (1979) and Hirshleifer (1988) combined the two
L68@P1: factors of hedging pressure and systematic risk to provide better model explanatory power. When considering systematic
L69@P1: risk, Carter et al. (1983) and Bessembinder (1992) used the indicator of hedging pressure to conduct empirical research
L70@P1: on futures prices, finding that hedging pressure will indeed influence futures prices and determining hedging pressure
L71@P1: to be a factor that can measure changes in futures prices. De Roon et al. (2000) further conducted cross-market research,
L72@P1: separating markets into four categories (the financial, agricultural, mineral, and currency markets), finding that the
L73@P1: prices of futures are not only influenced by the hedging pressure in their respective markets, but also by cross-hedging
L74@P1: pressure from different markets. In view of the above literature, this study carried out both same-market and crossmarket research, assuming that hedging pressure has a significant positive correlation with futures risk premium. In
L75@P1: addition, De Roon et al. (2000) studied the relationship between hedging pressure and futures prices in the period from
L76@P1: January 1986 to December 1994, 25 years before this study, making it necessary to demonstrate the applicability of past
L77@P1: research findings to the current situation of the futures market. As a result, this study first determined the validity of
L78@P1: past empirical results in a different research period.
L79@P1: In regard to literature on futures prices, in addition to the two factors of systematic risk and hedging pressure, other
L80@P1: scholars have used the amount of information owned by traders as a basis for measuring risk premium. Researchers in
L81@P1: this field believe that traders can more accurately predict product prices due to having a better understanding of market
L82@P1: conditions. Consequently, when unreasonable prices arise in the futures market, traders tend to choose to invest in the
L83@P1: market to acquire profits. For example, Stulz (1996) and Knill et al. (2006) believe that the routine business activities
L84@P1: of traders give them an advantage over other market participants by allowing them to more accurately predict price
L85@P1: fluctuations and therefore receive positive returns in the futures market.
L86@P1: Information asymmetry and product price formation make up the core of market microstructure research.
L87@P1: Regarding the measurement of information asymmetry in the futures market, Knill et al. (2006) used analysts’ revenue
L88@P1: forecasts for energy companies to measure the degree of information asymmetry in the futures market, finding that
L89@P1: degree of information asymmetry influences futures market prices. Concentration has been a factor seldom discussed
L90@P1: in research on futures markets in the past. When the open interest of futures contracts is concentrated in the hands of a
L91@P1-2: small number of buyers (sellers), this indicates that a small number of buyers (sellers) hold relatively greater market Market Concentration and Risk Premium 117
L92@P2: power and that traders may be able to manipulate futures prices to obtain profit and may also imply the forming of
L93@P2: information asymmetry. This paper constitutes the first study to explore the influence of futures contract concentration
L94@P2: on risk premium.
L95@P2: This study used market concentration as a basis to discuss whether information asymmetry exists in the futures
L96@P2: market and aims to determine whether trader concentration influences futures market prices. Changes in trader
L97@P2: concentration may suggest that traders have obtained private information, which allows them to increase their net long
L98@P2: (net short) futures positions and subsequently obtain positive returns in the futures market. This study used the
L99@P2: concentration data of the Commitments of Traders (COT) report of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
L100@P2: to find out whether information asymmetry exists in the US futures market. Concentration of traders was measured by
L101@P2: the difference between the concentration of net long positions and net short positions, When the concentration of traders
L102@P2: is positive (negative) in value, this means that futures prices will increase (decrease). Based on the above literature, we
L103@P2: can therefore expect that trader concentration has a significant positive correlation with futures risk premium.
L104@P2: Lastly, because the hedging pressure theory established by the research of Keynes (1930), Hicks (1939),
L105@P2: Houthakker (1957), and Cootner (1960) did not consider information asymmetry, the explanatory powers for risk
L106@P2: premium of hedging pressure and information asymmetry may differ under different futures markets. For example,
L107@P2: while spot pressure is unlikely to occur in financial markets, the expected harvesting times for crops in agricultural
L108@P2: markets will, in comparison, produce much greater hedging pressure. Therefore, this study asserts that discussion on
L109@P2: the factors that influence risk premium should simultaneously consider information asymmetry and hedging pressure.
L110@P2: In summary, there has yet to be any scholarship that has used market concentration to measure information asymmetry
L111@P2: or to simultaneously include information asymmetry and hedging pressure in models when discussing the influence of
L112@P2: information asymmetry and hedging pressure regarding risk premium. Whether changes in the market concentration of
L113@P2: informed traders can be used as a factor to explain futures risk premium is thus the primary objective of this study.
L114@P2: Moreover, whether the market concentration used in this study has better explanatory power for futures risk premium
L115@P2: than the hedging pressure focused on in past studies is also another point of emphasis of this study.
L116@P2: After the testing of the subjects selected for this study (the US’s financial futures market, agricultural futures market,
L117@P2: mineral futures market, and currency futures markets for the period from 2010 to 2018), we found that the market
L118@P2: concentration of the top four traders influences the prices of futures. Because traders who hold more futures contract
L119@P2: positions usually have more market information, they have a greater ability to predict price fluctuations. Additionally,
L120@P2: after the market concentration indicator and the hedging pressure indicator used by past scholars were put into the same
L121@P2: regression model, the predictiveness for futures prices showed a significant increase. The market concentration used in
L122@P2: this study thus provides another indicator for past literature to use in the explanation of futures return, whereby the
L123@P2: changes in futures return for some futures products that were unable to be explained using hedging pressure can be
L124@P2: predicted through market concentration. Lastly, this study found that for both hedging pressure and market concentration,
L125@P2: long-term predictions are always advantageous to short-term predictions, confirming that hedgers will invest in the
L126@P2: futures market to hedge in order to avoid risk and that information response does not occur in a short period of time.
L127@P2: The above results are expected to provide a significant amount of practical assistance to the devising of futures
L128@P2: investment strategies by market investors, formulation of trade regulations by policymakers, and prevention of market
L129@P2: manipulation, and to help to establish a more efficient and fair-trading environment for the futures market. The
L130@P2: subsequent framework for this study is as follows: the second chapter deals with sources; the third chapter is an
L131@P2: introduction to research methods; the fourth chapter presents empirical results and analysis; and the fifth chapter is a
L132@P2: conclusion based on the empirical results collected by this study.
L133@P2: 2. Sources
L134@P2: 2.1 Samples and Information Sources
L135@P2: The research period for this study was from January 1, 2010, to December 31, 2018, averting the 2008 financial
L136@P2: crisis to prevent the systematic influence of this period from affecting the research results. CFTC is the competent
L137@P2: authority for futures transactions, while the COT is a report published by the CFTC every Friday that aggregates the
L138@P2: open interest distributions of traders from when the market closes on Tuesday of the same week. Because the market
L139@P2: concentration data from the CFTC’s COT reports are provided once a week, the data frequency for this study is weekly.
L140@P2: The hedging pressure and concentration data used in this study were obtained from the CFTC’s COT reports, while the
L141@P2: recent month price data for all futures was obtained from Datastream. The futures markets in this study mainly included
L142@P2: the following: the financial futures market (including S&P index, T-bonds, and Eurodollars), the agricultural futures
L143@P2: market (including wheat, corn, soybean, and live cattle), the mineral futures market (including gold, silver, platinum,
L144@P2: and crude oil), and the currency futures market (including the Swiss franc, British pound, Japanese yen, and Canadian
L145@P2: dollar). The above research targets were chosen based on the research of De Roon et al. (2000) and constitute active and
L146@P2: important representatives for the futures of each market. COT reports have also been used by much past research on
L147@P2: hedging pressure for the carrying out of analysis (Chang et al., 2013; Chen & Yang, 2021; De Roon et al., 2000; Smales,
L148@P2-3: 2016; Wang, 2003).118 Management Review, Jul 2023

L150@P3: 2.2.1 Commercial and non-commercial positions
L151@P3: When traders buy and sell futures products, traders that use the futures contracts for some products to engage in
L152@P3: hedging behaviors as defined under CFTC Regulation 1.3, 17 CFR 1.3(z) have all their reported futures positions
L153@P3: classified as commercial positions, whereas traders not categorized as commercial traders are classified in the report as
L154@P3: non-commercial traders. The COT example provided in Figure 1 can be referenced as an example.

L157@P3: 2.2.2 The net position concentrations of the four top traders
L158@P3: The CFTC’s COT reports point out that the percentage of open interest held by the four top traders for each futures
L159@P3: product, regardless of whether the nature of transactions is commercial or non-commercial, is divided into gross long
L160@P3: positions and gross short positions. Concentration data is obtained through the net long positions and net short positions,
L161@P3: whereby net position concentration is the value obtained after gross long position and gross short position have offset
L162@P3: each other for the futures product of a given trader. Because trader concentration in regard to the 4 top traders does not
L163@P3: differentiate between commercial and non-commercial traders, the top traders may fall under either commercial or noncommercial classifications.

L175@P3: 2.3.2 Futures market concentration
L176@P3: When new market information is released, all investors will accordingly determine their response strategies. Using
L177@P3: the positive (negative) information in the stock market as an example, investors may collectively enter the long (short)
L178@P3: positions of the futures market. In such circumstances, although the total number of net long positions (short positions)
L179@P3: will increase, the market concentration of the top four traders is unlikely to change because the proportion of net long
L180@P3: (net short) positions held by traders remained unaffected. On the other hand, when new market information contains
L181@P3: uncertainties, risk-seeking investors may respectively enter long positions or short positions in the futures market, while
L182@P3: risk-averse investors may choose to liquidate their open positions. In a situation such as this, the trader concentration of
L183@P3: net long positions and net short positions may simultaneously increase. However, traders who hold more positions often
L184@P3: tend to have more market information. When highly exclusive information is acquired, they are likely to change the
L185@P3-4: quantity of their net long or short positions but other traders will, as a rule, not follow suit, causing changes to market Market Concentration and Risk Premium 119

L198@P4: 3. Research Methods and Model
L199@P4: This paper primarily used the model of De Roon et al. (2000) as its basis. De Roon et al. (2000) believed that
L200@P4: futures risk premium is influenced by market risk and hedging pressure from the same market. In addition, De Roon et
L201@P4: al. (2000) further proposed that, besides own-market hedging pressure, futures risk premium is influenced by crossmarket hedging pressure. De Roon et al. (2000) pointed out that the measurement of risk premium originates from the
L202@P4: difference between future spot prices and current futures prices. Because, in theory, future spot prices and current futures
L203@P4: prices should converge, the return gained from futures products is a good measurement index for futures risk premium.
L204@P4: In addition, futures do not have transaction costs during the initial period. According to the investment portfolio theory,
L205@P4: in the exclusion of risk-free assets, excess returns are equivalent to futures returns and risk premium refers to past
L206@P4: average excess returns. Consequently, this study used futures return as a proxy variable for risk premium to explore the
L207@P4: impact of hedging pressure and concentration on risk premium.

L1271@P14: 5. Conclusion
L1272@P14: This paper discusses the relationship between risk premium and market concentration in the United States’ futures
L1273@P14: market. Past research primarily used the hedging behaviors of hedgers as the measurement for futures risk premium,
L1274@P14: while this study confirmed that market concentration influences the prices of futures because traders who hold more
L1275@P14: futures contract positions usually have more market information and thus have a better ability to predict price
L1276@P14: fluctuations. When the market concentration for the previous top four traders increase, a rise in net open positions has
L1277@P14: a significant positive correlation with recent month futures risk premium, whereas an increase in net short positions has
L1278@P14: a significant negative correlation with recent month futures risk premium.
L1279@P14: Market concentration and hedging pressure measure different aspects. Market concentration measures the degree
L1280@P14: of information asymmetry in the futures market and hedging pressure measures the hedging behaviors engaged in by
L1281@P14: investors who hold or will hold spot stocks. Under the condition that market concentration and hedging pressure are
L1282@P14: simultaneously considered, market concentration retains its significance in the prediction of futures prices. As a result,
L1283@P14: market concentration provides another indicator for past literature to use in forming explanations regarding futures risk
